                                      PROJECT NO. 58482

           LARGE LOAD                                §            BEFORE THE
       DEMAND MANAGEMENT                             §     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
            SERVICE                                  §             OF TEXAS


  ENCHANTED ROCK, LLC’s COMMENTS TO COMMISSION STAFF’S MARCH 23
               MEMO AND QUESTIONS FOR COMMENT

       Enchanted Rock, LLC. (“Enchanted Rock”) appreciates the careful consideration being
given to establish the service for large load demand management under PURA § 39.170(b).
       Enchanted Rock is a Houston-based microgrid owner, operator, and developer with over
330 dual-purpose microgrids in operation throughout the state, providing over 560 MW of gas-
fired, dispatchable capacity to the Texas grid. Enchanted Rock is also operational in states across
the country in support of critical facilities and large loads. Enchanted Rock encourages the
Commission to consider the following comments regarding the implementation of the large load
demand management service.

COMMENTS

Question 1: Of the two options described in the attached slides, an as-needed service or a
seasonal service, which is the better option to implement PURA § 39.170(b) and why?

       A seasonal construct is the more effective approach to implement PURA § 39.170(b), as it
provides a stable and predictable framework that supports participation and investment in demand-
side flexibility. A seasonal program aligns with ERCOT’s existing Emergency Response Service
(ERS) construct and offers a forward signal that enables participants to make operational and
capital planning decisions. By contrast, an as-needed structure risks under-procurement and
limited participation, as it does not provide sufficient certainty for entities to develop and commit
reliable resources.
       This approach is also more consistent with the statutory requirement that the service be
“competitively procure[d]” as a reliability service. PURA § 39.170(b) contemplates a structured
procurement mechanism with defined availability periods and obligations, not ad hoc or
discretionary dispatch constructs. A seasonal framework better satisfies this requirement by
enabling competitive solicitation, qualification, and commitment processes analogous to existing
ERCOT reliability services.

                                                 1
         Prior attempts by ERCOT to procure needed demand response megawatts through ad hoc
or short-duration procurements have been unsuccessful, largely because they did not provide
sufficient lead time for entities to plan, develop, or contract for firm resources. Additionally, the
short-duration and uncertain nature of those procurements failed to create a sustainable investment
signal for the types of resources that can reliably commit to flexibility, i.e., large loads supported
by dispatchable generation-backed configurations. While certain load types, such as crypto mining
or steel mills, may be able to curtail in response to short-term signals, very few loads are able or
willing to curtail economically on a consistent basis. Firm loads, including critical manufacturing
facilities and data centers, often face extremely high opportunity costs to curtail operations.
        From a statutory perspective, this distinction is material. PURA § 39.170(b) requires
sustained curtailment for the duration of an Energy Emergency Alert (“EEA”) event, which implies
a level of operational firmness and reliability that cannot be satisfied by opportunistic or purely
price-responsive load reductions. Accordingly, the program design must prioritize resources
capable of delivering firm, dispatchable performance.
        Further, diesel generation deployments are generally constrained by federal air permit
limitations on non-emergency run hours and therefore cannot reliably participate in a program
intended to provide planned, dispatchable flexibility.1
        In practice, the resources most capable of providing reliable and scalable demand-side
flexibility are large loads that deploy on-site gas generation or storage and can respond to ERCOT
dispatch without interrupting core operations. These dispatchable, generation-backed load
configurations provide a more dependable form of participation at reasonable cost and should be
the primary target of program design.
        This outcome is consistent with broader legislative policy reflected in Senate Bill (“SB”)
6, including the objective of encouraging new dispatchable generation resources and reducing
reliance on involuntary load shed. Structuring the service to incent co-located generation or storage
investment aligns with that policy objective without requiring out-of-market subsidies.
        The most efficient and lowest-risk path to implementation is to build upon and expand the
existing ERS framework to satisfy the requirements of SB6. ERS provides a proven mechanism


1
 For example, the Department of Energy (“DOE”) issued emergency 202(c) orders for regions across the country to
waive emissions limits on generators so that they could operate in anticipation of energy emergencies arising from
Winter Storm Fern. The air permit waivers were required to call the backup generation ahead of firm load shed. See
https://www.energy.gov/documents/order-no-202-26-01-ercot.

                                                        2
 for procuring demand-side reliability services, with established qualification, telemetry, and
dispatch protocols. Rather than creating a duplicative or fragmented product, the Commission
should direct ERCOT to expand ERS to include a sub-product capable of meeting the statute’s 24-
hour notice requirement, thereby leveraging an existing, functional structure while accommodating
the specific requirements of PURA § 39.170(b).
       This approach is also consistent with the Commission’s authority under PURA § 39.151 to
direct ERCOT to implement reliability services through its Protocols, rather than creating a
separate regulatory construct outside of existing market frameworks.
       To ensure sufficient participation and support investment in dispatchable, generation-
backed load resources, the Commission should eliminate the existing fixed budget cap on the
program. Instead, procurement should be based on a target quantity of demand flexibility,
expressed in megawatts (MW) that reflects system reliability needs relative to total system peak.
Budget-constrained procurement risks suppressing participation, limiting competition, and
undermining the program’s effectiveness. A structure tied to reliability targets would better ensure
that sufficient resources are procured to meet evolving system conditions.
       A quantity-based procurement construct is also more consistent with reliability planning
practices reflected in ERCOT’s Capacity, Demand, and Reserves (“CDR”) process and avoids
introducing ratemaking-type constraints into what is intended to be a competitive reliability
service.

Question 2a: Does PURA authorize ERCOT to deploy the new service in circumstances other
than extreme weather events? If yes, what kind of events?

       PURA § 39.170(b) requires the Commission to establish rules governing deployment of
the service “in the event of an anticipated emergency condition,” and further requires that those
rules “must specify the periods when the service may be used…during extreme weather events.”

       Extreme weather events and EEAs are not always coincident events. Both subsections
(b)(1) and (b)(2) are not constraining on how the program can be used. It would seem reasonable
that a long lead-time flexible resource may also need to be called and/or deployed “to help prevent




                                                 3
 or alleviate2” an extreme weather event or EEA to help avoid load shed events. This type of
approach would be consistent with the Commission’s current policy on the use of ERS.3

          These provisions must be read together and given operative effect. The statute authorizes
deployment in connection with anticipated emergency conditions but requires that the Commission
define and limit the periods of use to those associated with extreme weather events. Accordingly,
the statute does not support an interpretation that would allow unrestricted deployment during any
EEA or general reliability condition.

          However, the term “anticipated emergency condition” is not defined in PURA § 39.170(b),
which necessarily confers a measure of interpretive discretion on the Commission in implementing
the statute. That discretion, however, is not unbounded; it must be exercised in a manner that is
consistent with the surrounding statutory text, including the requirement in subsection (b)(1) that
the rules “must specify the periods when the service may be used…during extreme weather
events.” Accordingly, any definition of “anticipated emergency condition” must be anchored to
forward-looking reliability conditions that are causally and temporally connected to extreme
weather events, rather than generalized system stress or routine operating conditions.

          Within that constraint, the Commission may reasonably interpret “anticipated emergency
condition” to encompass pre-event reliability risks identified through ERCOT’s forecasting,
planning, and operational processes, including conditions where system margins are expected to
deteriorate due to forecasted extreme temperatures, correlated outages, fuel constraints, or
transmission limitations associated with a pending weather event. In this context, the term
“anticipated” is most appropriately understood to refer to conditions that are identifiable in
advance based on objective system indicators—such as load forecasts, reserve margins, weather
projections, or known system constraints—and that present a credible risk of escalating into an
EEA if unmitigated.

          This interpretation is consistent with existing Commission policy and ERCOT operating
practices, which recognize that reliability tools may be deployed not only in response to active
emergency conditions, but also proactively “to help prevent or alleviate” such conditions before



2
    PUCT Substantive Rules § 25.507(b)
3
    See PUC Proj. No. 53493, Emergency Response Service, Order Adopting New § 25.507 (Aug. 4, 2022).

                                                        4
 firm load shed becomes necessary. Indeed, the inclusion of a mandatory 24-hour notice
requirement in PURA § 39.170(b)(2) further supports a forward-looking construct, as it
presupposes that the triggering condition can be identified sufficiently in advance to allow for
planned deployment, rather than real-time emergency intervention.

       At the same time, the Commission should ensure that any definition does not expand the
concept of “anticipated emergency condition” to encompass ordinary reliability management or
economic dispatch considerations. An interpretation that permits deployment based solely on
generalized system tightness, price signals, or non-weather-related contingencies would risk
severing the required nexus to extreme weather events and could render subsection (b)(1)’s
limiting language ineffective. Such an outcome would raise concerns under established canons of
statutory construction, including the obligation to give effect to all provisions of the statute and to
avoid interpretations that render statutory language superfluous.

       Accordingly, a legally defensible implementation would define “anticipated emergency
condition” as a forecasted reliability condition, reasonably expected to occur within a defined
temporal window, that is driven by or directly associated with an impending extreme weather event
and that, absent intervention, is likely to result in an EEA or firm load shed. This approach
preserves the Commission’s necessary operational flexibility while maintaining fidelity to the
statutory structure and constraints established by PURA § 39.170(b). Importantly, this discretion
is not unbounded. Any interpretation that extends deployment beyond weather-linked reliability
conditions would risk exceeding the Commission’s delegated authority and rendering the statutory
reference to “extreme weather events” superfluous.

Question 2b: Should the commission define “extreme weather event” and, if so, how should it
be defined?

       A definition of “extreme weather event” should be included; however, it should be
sufficiently flexible to preserve ERCOT’s ability to respond to evolving system conditions. A
narrowly prescriptive definition would risk constraining ERCOT’s operational discretion in a
manner inconsistent with its reliability mandate under PURA § 39.151. Conversely, the definition
should remain tethered to objectively identifiable weather-driven system stress conditions to
ensure compliance with PURA § 39.170(b)(1).



                                                  5
 Question 3a: What type of qualification is necessary to show that it may take a large load
customer 24 hours to ramp down safely?

       Enchanted Rock has no comment at this time.

Question 3b: What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should
apply to participation in the new service?

       Any additional prohibitions should be narrowly tailored to ensure that participating
resources represent firm, dispatchable, and legally deployable capability, consistent with the
reliability purpose of PURA § 39.170(b), while avoiding expansion beyond the Commission’s
delegated authority.

       At a minimum, participating loads should be required to demonstrate that any on-site
generation or storage relied upon to provide flexibility is fully permitted and capable of operating
for the duration of a deployment without reliance on emergency regulatory waivers. As noted,
resources that require emergency air permit waivers to perform cannot be considered firm or
reliably dispatchable and therefore should not be eligible to participate.

       Beyond this constraint, additional prohibitions should be approached cautiously. PURA §
39.170(b)(3) already specifies key participation limits, including prohibitions on price-responsive
curtailment and participation in other reliability or ancillary services. Expanding the scope of
prohibitions beyond those expressly identified in the statute risks introducing requirements that
may not be supported by legislative authorization and could deter participation without a
commensurate reliability benefit.

       Accordingly, any supplemental restrictions should be limited to objective, reliability-based
criteria—such as verifiable performance capability, telemetry, and operational readiness—and
should not introduce broader policy-based exclusions that are not grounded in the statutory
framework.




                                                 6
 Question 3c: Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four
coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new service?

        No, but only under properly tailored interpretation of PURA § 39.170(b)(3) that
distinguishes between price-responsive load curtailment and the provision of reliability services
through dispatchable, generation-backed flexibility.

        PURA § 39.170(b)(3) prohibits participation by large load customers that “curtail[] in
response to the wholesale price of electricity” or that participate in other reliability or ancillary
services. This prohibition is appropriately applied to loads whose participation is based on
discretionary curtailment in response to economic signals, including wholesale price exposure or
transmission-based constructs such as 4CP.

        However, the price responsiveness evaluation should not apply to large loads that are
bidding in flexibility to the new service through their investment in co-located dispatchable
generation or storage (i.e., “bring your own generation” or BYOG configurations). In such cases,
the resource is not curtailing load in response to price; rather, it is providing a reliability service
through controllable, dispatchable supply capability located behind the meter.).

        This distinction is critical. In the former case—pure load curtailment—there has been
significant discussion and debate regarding whether certain load types are effectively monetizing
volatility by reducing consumption in response to price signals, without providing firm or
dispatchable reliability value—e.g., crypto mining operations profiting from “solving a problem
they created.”4 The statutory prohibition on price-responsive participation appropriately addresses
that concern.

        By contrast, in the BYOG context, the new service functions as an investment signal to
drive the development of new dispatchable resources by new large loads entering Texas. The signal
is for large loads to invest in new on-site generation or storage that can: i) maintain continuity of
operations during grid outages or load shed events, and (ii) provide reliable, dispatchable support
to the grid when called upon. This form of participation is fundamentally different from price-




5
 Reply Brief and Protest of Enchanted Rock, LLC in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s initial brief (EL25-
49 et al) (Feb. 23, 2026) at https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/filedownload?fileid=19B4DFD8-7877-C8A5-A3DE-
9D2690800000.

                                                       7
 responsive curtailment because it reflects committed, infrastructure-backed capability rather than
opportunistic behavior.

       Moreover, facilitating BYOG participation aligns with broader state policy objectives to
encourage the development of new dispatchable generation resources, including through programs
such as the Texas Energy Fund. The principal distinction is that, in this context, the investment is
being driven directly by new large load customers rather than through centralized procurement or
subsidy structures.

       Accordingly, the Commission should clarify that the prohibition in PURA § 39.170(b)(3)
applies to load curtailment behavior driven by price signals, but does not apply to participation
based on dispatchable capability provided through co-located generation or storage. The
evaluation framework should be structured to distinguish between these two modes of participation
in a manner that is objective, administrable, and consistent with ERCOT market constructs.

Question 3d: Should the commission define “curtailment in response to wholesale price of
electricity” and, if so, how should it be defined?

       ERCOT is currently working on a price responsiveness test in its evaluation of ERS
program design reform options. While ERCOT is considering the use of the test on all resources,
Enchanted Rock urges the Commission to utilize the test for load curtailments strictly. As noted in
response to Question 3(c), the test should not apply to customers who are participating with
flexibility created by investment in new dispatchable generation and storage on-site

Question 4: How should the target quantity, budget, and price be set for the new service? What
additional information should the Commission consider in its implementation of PURA §
39.170(b)?

       See response to Question 1.

Question 5: Should the Commission include in this rulemaking a directive implementing PURA
§39.170(a)?

       Given the rapid innovation cycle on large load architecture and co-location designs, the
Commission should address standardized curtailment protocols and equipment and technology
requirements in a separate proceeding.



                                                 8
           This separation is appropriate because subsection (a) establishes mandatory curtailment
capability requirements, while subsection (b) establishes a voluntary, competitively procured
reliability service. Conflating these frameworks risks distorting both program design and statutory
intent.

          That said, when it comes to the coordination of load shed activities with the new service
contemplated by SB 6, the Commission should ensure that for large load customers that have
deployed co-located generation or storage sufficient to offset their grid consumption, compliance
with reliability obligations is satisfied through the dispatch of those on-site resources, rather than
requiring simultaneous curtailment of the underlying load.

          For example, for a 100 MW large load that has installed 100 MW of on-site dispatchable
generation or storage, the obligation to provide 100 MW of demand reduction should be satisfied
by dispatching that on-site capability. If the load is additionally required to curtail its consumption
while simultaneously dispatching its on-site resources, the result is a 200 MW response to the
grid—100 MW from generation and 100 MW from load reduction—while the facility itself is
forced offline.

          This outcome is neither economically rational nor consistent with the purpose of PURA §
39.170(b), which is to procure reliable demand reductions—not to require duplicative or punitive
performance that exceeds the resource’s committed capability. It also undermines the investment
signal for co-located generation and storage by preventing the customer from utilizing those assets
for business continuity during reliability events.

          This issue has been identified in wholesale market regions throughout the country
evaluating similar co-located load and generation configurations. For example, Enchanted Rock
and others, in PJM Interconnection LLC (“PJM”) proceedings, have raised concerns that
curtailment constructs which prohibit the use of co-located generation can render such
configurations commercially impractical and inconsistent with reliability objectives.5

          Accordingly, the Commission should clarify that, where a large load demonstrates that it
can fully offset its grid demand through on-site dispatchable resources, deployment instructions

5
 Reply Brief and Protest of Enchanted Rock, LLC in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s initial brief (EL25-
49 et al) (Feb. 23, 2026) at https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/filedownload?fileid=19B4DFD8-7877-C8A5-A3DE-
9D2690800000.

                                                       9
 under the § 39.170(b) service or under load shed protocols should not require additional
curtailment of the underlying load. This approach preserves alignment between obligation and
capability, avoids double counting of reliability contributions, and maintains the economic
rationale for investment in dispatchable, co-located infrastructure.

CONCLUSION

       Enchanted Rock appreciates the opportunity to submit these responses to Commission
Staff’s questions regarding implementation of PURA § 39.170(b), the large load demand
management service. The Commission has a critical opportunity to establish a reliability service
that both enhances grid reliability and supports long-term investment in dispatchable resources.

       A properly structured, seasonal, ERS-based construct—aligned with statutory constraints,
grounded in ERCOT operational frameworks, and designed to incentivize new dispatchable
capacity—will best achieve the Legislature’s objectives while maintaining market integrity and
regulatory consistency.

       Equally important, the Commission should maintain a clear separation between the
voluntary, competitively procured reliability service contemplated by PURA § 39.170(b) and the
mandatory curtailment framework established under PURA § 39.170(a), including any associated
“kill switch” or direct load control requirements. These two constructs serve fundamentally
different purposes: subsection (a) establishes baseline reliability obligations applicable to large
loads during firm load shed, while subsection (b) is intended to create forward-looking incentives
for voluntary, dispatchable demand-side participation.

       Conflating these frameworks risks undermining both. Incorporating mandatory curtailment
policy elements into the design of the § 39.170(b) service could distort participation incentives,
introduce uncertainty regarding performance obligations, and weaken the investment signal for co-
located generation and storage. Conversely, developing subsection (a) requirements within the
context of this proceeding may prematurely constrain technology, operational design, and
implementation pathways that warrant separate, focused stakeholder engagement.

       Accordingly, the Commission should proceed with implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)
as a distinct, market-based reliability service, while addressing subsection (a) through a separate
process that allows for more detailed technical, operational, and policy development. This

                                                10
 approach preserves clarity of purpose, ensures alignment with statutory intent, and supports
efficient and durable program design.

       Enchanted Rock remains committed to working with the Commission and ERCOT to
support the development of a reliability framework that improves system resiliency and stability,
while enabling continued investment and innovation in large load and co-located resource
configurations.


                                                    Respectfully submitted,

                                                    /s/ Joel Yu

                                                    Joel Yu
                                                    Senior VP, Policy & External Affairs
                                                    Enchanted Rock, LLC.
                                                    jyu@enchantedrock.com

                                         EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
   Adopt Seasonal Procurement Structure
       o Implement a seasonal, forward procurement construct rather than an as-needed approach
       o Ensure participation certainty, operational planning, and investment in reliable resources
   Leverage Existing ERS Framework
       o Direct ERCOT to expand ERS (including a sub-product) to satisfy § 39.170(b)
       o Avoid creation of duplicative or fragmented program structures
   Procure to Reliability Need (MW-Based), Not Budget
       o Eliminate fixed budget caps
       o Establish MW procurement targets tied to system reliability (e.g., CDR / peak demand)
       o Prevent under-procurement and support adequate participation
   Prioritize Dispatchable, Generation-Backed Flexibility (BYOG)
        o Focus on firm, infrastructure-backed capability rather than discretionary load curtailment
        o Recognize co-located generation and storage (BYOG) as preferred participation model
        o Support investment in new dispatchable resources consistent with SB 6 policy objectives
   Clarify Price Responsiveness Prohibition
       o Apply prohibition only to price-driven load curtailment behavior
       o Confirm that BYOG participation is not “curtailment,” but provision of a reliability service
       o Permit participation alongside constructs such as 4CP, where not price-driven
       o Limit any ERCOT price responsiveness test to load behavior only
   Define “Anticipated Emergency Condition” Within Statutory Bounds
       o Interpret as forecasted, forward-looking reliability conditions tied to extreme weather
       o Allow pre-event deployment to prevent or mitigate imminent emergency conditions
   Define “Extreme Weather Event” with Flexibility and Constraint
       o Provide a definition that is operationally flexible but tied to weather-driven system stress
       o Preserve ERCOT discretion while maintaining statutory limits under § 39.170(b)(1)
   Ensure Participation Reflects Firm, Permitted Capability
       o Require resources to be fully permitted and operable without emergency waivers
       o Limit additional participation restrictions to objective, reliability-based criteria
       o Avoid expanding beyond statutory prohibitions in § 39.170(b)(3)
   Avoid Market Distortion
       o Avoid structuring as an out-of-market or make-whole construct
       o Preserve price signals and competitive market outcomes
   Prevent Double Counting of Reliability Contributions
       o Clarify that dispatch of on-site generation satisfies the load’s obligation
       o Prohibit requirements for simultaneous load curtailment and generation dispatch
       o Avoid outcomes where a 100 MW load is forced to provide 200 MW of response
       o Preserve economic value of co-located resources for business continuity
   Maintain Separation from § 39.170(a) (“Kill Switch”)
       o Preserve distinction between: § 39.170(a): mandatory curtailment capability; and § 39.170(b): voluntary,
           market-based reliability service
       o Develop “kill switch” policy in a separate, dedicated proceeding
   Align with ERCOT Operational Framework
        o Ensure integration with existing ERCOT Protocols, dispatch, and telemetry systems
        o Avoid creating parallel or conflicting operational obligations

         However, the term "anticipated emergency condition" is not defined in PURA § 39.170(b),
which necessarily confers a measure of interpretive discretion on the Commission in implementing
the statute. That discretion, however, is not unbounded; it must be exercised in a manner that is
consistent with the surrounding statutory text, including the requirement in subsection (b)(1) that
the rules "must specify the periods when the service may be used... during extreme weather
events." Accordingly, any definition of "anticipated emergency condition" must be anchored to
forward-looking reliability conditions that are causally and temporally connected to extreme
weather events, rather than generalized system stress or routine operating conditions.

         Within that constraint, the Commission may reasonably interpret "anticipated emergency
condition" to encompass pre-event reliability risks identified through ERCOT's forecasting,
planning, and operational processes, including conditions where system margins are expected to
deteriorate due to forecasted extreme temperatures, correlated outages, fuel constraints, or
transmission limitations associated with a pending weather event. In this context, the term
"anticipated" is most appropriately understood to refer to conditions that are identifiable in
advance based on objective system indicators-such as load forecasts, reserve margins, weather
projections, or known system constraints-and that present a credible risk of escalating into an
EEA if unmitigated.

         This interpretation is consistent with existing Commission policy and ERCOT operating
practices, which recognize that reliability tools may be deployed not only in response to active
emergency conditions, but also proactively "to help prevent or alleviate" such conditions before

requirement in PURA § 39.170(b)(2) further supports a forward-looking construct, as it
presupposes that the triggering condition can be identified sufficiently in advance to allow for
planned deployment, rather than real-time emergency intervention.

       At the same time, the Commission should ensure that any definition does not expand the
concept of "anticipated emergency condition" to encompass ordinary reliability management or
economic dispatch considerations. An interpretation that permits deployment based solely on
generalized system tightness, price signals, or non-weather-related contingencies would risk
severing the required nexus to extreme weather events and could render subsection (b)(1)'s
limiting language ineffective. Such an outcome would raise concerns under established canons of
statutory construction, including the obligation to give effect to all provisions of the statute and to
avoid interpretations that render statutory language superfluous.

       Accordingly, a legally defensible implementation would define "anticipated emergency
condition" as a forecasted reliability condition, reasonably expected to occur within a defined
temporal window, that is driven by or directly associated with an impending extreme weather event
and that, absent intervention, is likely to result in an EEA or firm load shed. This approach
preserves the Commission's necessary operational flexibility while maintaining fidelity to the
statutory structure and constraints established by PURA § 39.170(b). Importantly, this discretion
is not unbounded. Any interpretation that extends deployment beyond weather-linked reliability
conditions would risk exceeding the Commission's delegated authority and rendering the statutory
reference to "extreme weather events" superfluous.

Question 2b: Should the commission define "extreme weather event" and, if so, how should it
be dejined?

       A definition of "extreme weather event" should be included; however, it should be
sufficiently flexible to preserve ERCOT's ability to respond to evolving system conditions. A
narrowly prescriptive definition would risk constraining ERCOT's operational discretion in a
manner inconsistent with its reliability mandate under PURA § 39.151. Conversely, the definition
should remain tethered to obj ectively identifiable weather-driven system stress conditions to
ensure compliance with PURA § 39.170(b)(1)

Question 3b: What specific prohibitions not enumerated in PURA § 39.170(b), if any, should
apply to participation in the new service?

       Any additional prohibitions should be narrowly tailored to ensure that participating
resources represent firm, dispatchable, and legally deployable capability, consistent with the
reliability purpose of PURA § 39.170(b), while avoiding expansion beyond the Commission's
delegated authority.

       At a minimum, participating loads should be required to demonstrate that any on-site
generation or storage relied upon to provide flexibility is fully permitted and capable of operating
for the duration of a deployment without reliance on emergency regulatory waivers. As noted,
resources that require emergency air permit waivers to perform cannot be considered firm or
reliably dispatchable and therefore should not be eligible to participate.

       Beyond this constraint, additional prohibitions should be approached cautiously. PURA §
39.170(b)(3) already specifies key participation limits, including prohibitions on price-responsive
curtailment and participation in other reliability or ancillary services. Expanding the scope of
prohibitions beyond those expressly identified in the statute risks introducing requirements that
may not be supported by legislative authorization and could deter participation without a
commensurate reliability benefit.

       Accordingly, any supplemental restrictions should be limited to obj ective, reliability-based
criteria-such as verifiable performance capability, telemetry, and operational readiness-and
should not introduce broader policy-based exclusions that are not grounded in the statutory
framework.

 Question 3c: Should participation in price responsiveness to transmission scarcity such as four
coincident peak (4CP) or a successor methodology preclude participation in the new service?

        No, but only under properly tailored interpretation of PURA § 39.170(b)(3) that
distinguishes between price-responsive load curtailment and the provision of reliability services
through dispatchable, generation-backed flexibility.

        PURA § 39.170(b)(3) prohibits participation by large load customers that "curtail[I in
response to the wholesale price of electricity" or that participate in other reliability or ancillary
services. This prohibition is appropriately applied to loads whose participation is based on
discretionary curtailment in response to economic signals, including wholesale price exposure or
transmission-based constructs such as 4CP.

        However, the price responsiveness evaluation should not apply to large loads that are
bidding in flexibility to the new service through their investment in co-located dispatchable
generation or storage (i.e., "bring your own generation" or BYOG configurations). In such cases,
the resource is not curtailing load in response to price; rather, it is providing a reliability service
through controllable, dispatchable supply capability located behind the meter.).

        This distinction is critical. In the former case-pure load curtailment-there has been
significant discussion and debate regarding whether certain load types are effectively monetizing
volatility by reducing consumption in response to price signals, without providing firm or
dispatchable reliability value-e.g., crypto mining operations profiting from "solving a problem
they created."4 The statutory prohibition on price-responsive participation appropriately addresses
that concern.

        By contrast, in the BYOG context, the new service functions as an investment signal to
drive the development of new dispatchable resources by new large loads entering Texas. The signal
is for large loads to invest in new on-site generation or storage that can: i) maintain continuity of
operations during grid outages or load shed events, and (ii) provide reliable, dispatchable support
to the grid when called upon. This form of participation is fundamentally different from price-

           This separation is appropriate because subsection (a) establishes mandatory curtailment
capability requirements, while subsection (b) establishes a voluntary, competitively procured
reliability service. Conflating these frameworks risks distorting both program design and statutory
intent.

          That said, when it comes to the coordination of load shed activities with the new service
contemplated by SB 6, the Commission should ensure that for large load customers that have
deployed co-located generation or storage sufficient to offset their grid consumption, compliance
with reliability obligations is satisfied through the dispatch of those on-site resources, rather than
requiring simultaneous curtailment of the underlying load.

          For example, for a 100 MW large load that has installed 100 MW of on-site dispatchable
generation or storage, the obligation to provide 100 MW of demand reduction should be satisfied
by dispatching that on-site capability. Ifthe load is additionally required to curtail its consumption
while simultaneously dispatching its on-site resources, the result is a 200 MW response to the
grid-100 MW from generation and 100 MW from load reduction-while the facility itself is
forced offline.

          This outcome is neither economically rational nor consistent with the purpose of PURA §
39.170(b), which is to procure reliable demand reductions-not to require duplicative or punitive
performance that exceeds the resource's committed capability. It also undermines the investment
signal for co-located generation and storage by preventing the customer from utilizing those assets
for business continuity during reliability events.

          This issue has been identified in wholesale market regions throughout the country
evaluating similar co-located load and generation configurations. For example, Enchanted Rock
and others, in PJM Interconnection LLC ("PJM') proceedings, have raised concerns that
curtailment constructs which prohibit the use of co-located generation can render such
configurations commercially impractical and inconsistent with reliability objectives.5

          Accordingly, the Commission should clarify that, where a large load demonstrates that it
can fully offset its grid demand through on-site dispatchable resources, deployment instructions

CONCLUSION

       Enchanted Rock appreciates the opportunity to submit these responses to Commission
Staff's questions regarding implementation of PURA § 39.170(b), the large load demand
management service. The Commission has a critical opportunity to establish a reliability service
that both enhances grid reliability and supports long-term investment in dispatchable resources.

       A properly structured, seasonal, ERS-based construct-aligned with statutory constraints,
grounded in ERCOT operational frameworks, and designed to incentivize new dispatchable
capacity-will best achieve the Legislature's objectives while maintaining market integrity and
regulatory consistency.

       Equally important, the Commission should maintain a clear separation between the
voluntary, competitively procured reliability service contemplated by PURA § 39.170(b) and the
mandatory curtailment framework established under PURA § 39.170(a), including any associated
"kill switch" or direct load control requirements. These two constructs serve fundamentally
different purposes: subsection (a) establishes baseline reliability obligations applicable to large
loads during firm load shed, while subsection (b) is intended to create forward-looking incentives
for voluntary, dispatchable demand-side participation.

       Conflating these frameworks risks undermining both. Incorporating mandatory curtailment
policy elements into the design of the § 39. 170(b) service could distort participation incentives,
introduce uncertainty regarding performance obligations, and weaken the investment signal for co-
located generation and storage. Conversely, developing subsection (a) requirements within the
context of this proceeding may prematurely constrain technology, operational design, and
implementation pathways that warrant separate, focused stakeholder engagement.

       Accordingly, the Commission should proceed with implementation of PURA § 39.170(b)
as a distinct, market-based reliability service, while addressing subsection (a) through a separate
process that allows for more detailed technical, operational, and policy development. This

 approach preserves clarity of purpose, ensures alignment with statutory intent, and supports
efficient and durable program design.

       Enchanted Rock remains committed to working with the Commission and ERCOT to
support the development of a reliability framework that improves system resiliency and stability,
while enabling continued investment and innovation in large load and co-located resource
configurations.
